notes: 9 of 10 evals pass 100% in both configurations — these assertions are non-discriminating and do not measure skill value. The only discriminating eval is simpsons-paradox (eval 8): without-skill scores 25% vs with-skill 100%.

Without-skill 92.5% ± 23.7%: the high stddev is entirely driven by the single failing eval (simpsons-paradox). Across the other 9 evals, baseline Claude already achieves 100% — suggesting most assertions are too easy or test general causal reasoning that the model already has.

Skill overhead: with-skill runs take ~43s longer on average (114.5s vs 71.5s) and use ~9,000 more tokens (~75% more). This overhead is constant across all evals due to the skill text being loaded into context.

The simpsons-paradox eval is the only eval that tests skill-specific behavior (DAG-dependent resolution of paradox, mediator vs confounder framing). Other evals test behaviors the base model already handles correctly (name the rung, identify DiD assumptions, recognize RDD threshold, etc.).

Recommendation: the eval set should be redesigned with harder assertions that test the specific behaviors the skill adds — particularly DAG junction identification, collider trap recognition, distinguishing mediators from confounders in concrete examples, and naming specific adjustment strategies. Consider replacing the 9 non-discriminating evals with harder variants.

Token cost tradeoff: adding the skill to context costs ~9,000 tokens per invocation but only improves one eval out of ten. If the skill is expected to be triggered often, the token cost needs to be justified by more discriminating performance gains.
